summary: Psalm 49 summons all people, rich and poor alike, to hear a wisdom teaching about wealth, death, and false security. It argues that riches cannot ransom a life or prevent decay, and it contrasts those who trust wealth with the speaker's confidence that God will redeem him from Sheol. The psalm ends by repeating that riches without understanding leave a person no better than animals that perish.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how the Psalter includes wisdom instruction, not only prayer and praise. Within Book II of Psalms, it gives a public reflection on the limits of wealth and the hope that God, not possessions, has final power over life.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with the sons of Korah and the Chief Musician; the broader Psalter includes many writers and collections, and headings can mark authorship, association, dedication, or belonging.
context.audience: The psalm directly addresses “all you peoples” and “all you inhabitants of the world,” including “both low and high, rich and poor together.”
context.date: Psalms is a many-period anthology; this individual psalm cannot be dated securely from its wording or heading alone.
context.setting: Book II of Psalms, a collection that includes Korahite, Asaphite, and Davidic material; this chapter is framed as public wisdom speech with musical language.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew wisdom poetry in the Psalter, using parallel lines, comparison, rhetorical question, and repeated conclusion.

outline.heading: A Worldwide Summons
outline.note: The speaker calls every social level to listen and presents the psalm as wisdom, understanding, proverb, and riddle.

outline.heading: The Question of Fear
outline.note: The psalm asks why the speaker should fear in evil days, since even the wealthy cannot ransom another life or buy escape from corruption.

outline.heading: Wealth Cannot Endure
outline.note: Wise, foolish, and senseless people all die, leave wealth behind, and fail to endure despite property and status.

outline.heading: The Destiny of the Foolish
outline.note: Those who approve this way of life are pictured as a flock for Sheol, while the speaker says God will redeem his soul from Sheol's power.

outline.heading: Do Not Fear the Rich
outline.note: The final section tells readers not to be afraid when someone grows rich, because glory does not follow the dead and wealth without understanding ends in perishability.

keyVerses.text: both low and high, rich and poor together.
keyVerses.why: This line shows that the psalm is not advice for one class only; it addresses everyone under the same reality.

keyVerses.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him.
keyVerses.why: This is the central claim about the limit of wealth: it cannot purchase another person's life from death.

keyVerses.text: But God will redeem my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me. Selah.
keyVerses.why: This line gives the psalm's strongest contrast to human wealth: God can do what money cannot.

keyVerses.text: A man who has riches without understanding, is like the animals that perish.
keyVerses.why: The final verse restates the psalm's warning in its sharpest form and closes the argument.

themes: the failure of ransom by riches

questions.question: Who is being addressed in this psalm?
questions.answer: The psalm addresses all people, not only Israel or one social group. Its opening summons includes “all you peoples,” “all you inhabitants of the world,” and then names both low and high, rich and poor together.

questions.question: What kind of psalm is this?
questions.answer: The speaker describes the speech as wisdom, understanding, a proverb, and a riddle. That makes the chapter read like instruction about how to understand life, wealth, and death, even though it remains a poem meant to be voiced or sung.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears after the warning about the foolish and again after the speaker's confidence that God will receive him. The exact force of this performance term is uncertain, so readers can note its placement without claiming to know precisely how it functioned.

questions.question: Why does the speaker say not to fear in evil days?
questions.answer: The fear described is connected to surrounding iniquity and to people who trust and boast in riches. The answer is not that danger is unreal, but that wealth cannot ultimately control life, death, or redemption.

questions.question: Does the psalm say wealth is evil by itself?
questions.answer: The chapter criticizes trusting in wealth, boasting in riches, and having riches without understanding. It does not say every rich person is automatically wicked; it warns that wealth can create false confidence because it cannot prevent death or follow a person after death.

questions.question: What does it mean that no one can “redeem” or pay a “ransom” for another?
questions.answer: In this psalm, redeeming and ransoming refer to securing a life from death or corruption. The point is that human wealth is insufficient: “no payment is ever enough” to make someone live forever.

questions.question: Is verse 15 teaching resurrection?
questions.answer: Readers differ on how far to press the line “God will redeem my soul from the power of Sheol.” At minimum, within the psalm, it contrasts God's power to receive the speaker with wealth's inability to rescue anyone from death. Later Jewish and Christian readers have connected such language with hope beyond death, but the chapter itself states the hope poetically rather than explaining a full doctrine.

questions.question: What is Sheol in this chapter?
questions.answer: Sheol is the place or realm associated with the dead in the poem. The psalm pictures the foolish as appointed there and says their beauty decays there, while the speaker trusts God to redeem his soul from its power.

questions.question: Why compare a rich person without understanding to animals?
questions.answer: The comparison appears in verses 12 and 20, with a difference in emphasis. Verse 12 says that human beings do not endure despite their riches; verse 20 specifically names a person with riches but without understanding. Both stress perishability and the limits of wealth, rather than denying human dignity in every respect.

glossary.def: The heading's phrase for the person or role connected with the psalm's performance; the exact original performance setting is not recoverable from this chapter alone.
The group named in the heading as associated with this psalm; the Psalter includes other Korahite material in Book II.
A compact wisdom saying or teaching form; here the speaker says he will incline his ear to one.
A difficult saying or problem to be worked through; the speaker says he will solve it on the harp.
The realm of the dead as pictured in this psalm, where death shepherds the foolish and from whose power the speaker trusts God to redeem him.
